The Government of India ended K.V. Subramanian's IMF ED term roughly six months before its scheduled October-2025 expiry. The IMF's spokesperson confirmed to Business Standard that the decision was the Indian government's, not the Fund's (documented as to WHO decided). The REASONS are less firmly sourced: Business Standard, citing an Indian Express report and unnamed sources, said Subramanian had raised concerns about IMF datasets (creating friction within the Fund) and that questions had been raised over his marketing/promotion of his book "India@100" while in the post; the recall also preceded an IMF board vote on financial assistance to Pakistan, which India was set to oppose. No official public reason was given by the Government of India. Tier set to alleged because the specific reasons rest on unnamed sourcing and directly imply impropriety by Subramanian.

claims.d: External-debt stock CAGR, UPA decade (2004-2014, US$123.6bn -> US$457.5bn) approx 14.0%/yr, vs NDA decade (2014-2024, US$457.5bn -> US$716.5bn) approx 4.6%/yr — World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.CD. Read naively this looks like NDA borrowed far more conservatively; the innocent reading below is why that comparison is not safe as stated.
claims.lab: UPA vs NDA external-debt growth rate (base-rate comparison)
claims.innocentReading: A percentage growth rate compounds off a much smaller 2004 base than the 2014 base, so a lower headline CAGR in the later decade is arithmetically expected even under identical policy; the stock is also a current-US$ figure, so rupee depreciation, global interest-rate cycles (the 2013 "taper tantrum" falls inside the UPA window) and the growth of private corporate/NRI external borrowing (not government policy at all) all move the number independently of which party held the finance portfolio.
claims.upgradeIf: A like-for-like comparison of sovereign-only (PPG) debt as % of GDP, not total stock in current US$, showed a persistent post-2014 discontinuity not explained by valuation or base effects.
claims.killIf: PPG debt/GDP shows no discontinuity across the 2014 transition (the World Bank PPG series fetched this session — $205bn in 2021 vs $215bn in 2023 — shows gradual, not stepped, change, weakly supporting kill).

narratives.claim: The 1991 reforms were dictated by the IMF.
narratives.strongestCase: The stand-by arrangement and CCFF drawdown coincided with, and were conditioned on, structural adjustment commitments — devaluation, de-licensing, opening protected sectors to foreign participation — and the government pledged national gold reserves as collateral to secure the loan, a strong signal of how constrained the negotiating position was.
narratives.strongestCounter: The core liberalisation package (industrial de-licensing, trade reform, the start of financial-sector opening) was designed by the Rao government's own economic team and framed domestically as a long-overdue correction to decades of licence-permit-raj inefficiency; several of these ideas had been debated inside the Indian policy establishment since the mid-1980s (Rajiv Gandhi-era partial liberalisation) independent of any IMF programme, and the reforms continued and deepened long after the 1991-93 facility was repaid, when the IMF had no further leverage.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A primary IMF or RBI document itemising the specific conditions attached to the 1991 facility, compared line-by-line against the reform sequence actually enacted, would let this be scored rather than asserted either way — not obtained this session (imf.org and dea.gov.in both blocked).

narratives.claim: India is heading for an external debt crisis.
narratives.strongestCase: The absolute stock has grown continuously and substantially — from US$101bn in 2000 to US$716bn in 2024, a roughly sevenfold increase — and short-term debt is a meaningful roughly one-fifth of the total, which is the maturity structure that turned into a crisis in 1991.
narratives.strongestCounter: External debt was 18.0% of GNI in 2023 and total debt service was 10.2% of exports in 2023 (World Bank), both moderate by international and by India's own 1991-era standards (when the debt-service ratio approached 30-35% of exports on a far smaller and more fragile reserve base); foreign-exchange reserves (not itemised in this file) have historically comfortably covered the stock; and the sovereign (public & publicly guaranteed) share of the debt has been shrinking as a proportion of the total relative to private/NRI-linked borrowing, which is a materially different risk profile from a government unable to service its own external obligations.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A sustained rise in the debt-service ratio past the 20-25% range historically associated with distress, or a sharp reserves drawdown alongside it, would move this out of "unsupported."

narratives.claim: The IMF/World Bank control Indian policy.
narratives.strongestCase: India has an active, continuous lending relationship with the World Bank (IBRD/IDA loans, detailed in the companion file worldbank-projects.json) that comes with project-level conditions, and the IMF's annual Article IV consultation produces policy recommendations that sometimes anticipate or echo budget measures.
narratives.strongestCounter: India has not drawn on IMF balance-of-payments financing — the channel that gives the Fund real leverage over macroeconomic policy — since the 1991-93 facility; Article IV consultations are surveillance and advice, not conditionality, and India is free to (and often does) ignore them; multilateral (IBRD+IDA) debt was only US$39.3bn of a US$647.6bn total external debt stock in 2023 (about 6%), a small enough share that project-level conditions on that slice cannot plausibly be read as "control" of national policy.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Evidence of a live use-of-Fund-resources arrangement with binding macro conditionality, or a demonstrated pattern of budget reversals directly traceable to World Bank loan conditions across multiple sectors, would move this out of "unsupported."

narratives.claim: India's IMF Executive Director (K.V. Subramanian) was removed for criticising the Fund / for misconduct.
narratives.strongestCase: Business Standard, citing an Indian Express report and unnamed sources, reported that Subramanian's early exit followed his having raised concerns about IMF datasets — friction with the Fund over substance — and separately that questions had been raised about his promoting his own book while in the post; the recall also came days before an IMF board vote on aid to Pakistan that India opposed, which some read as the more consequential trigger.
narratives.strongestCounter: The IMF itself told Business Standard on the record that ending his term was the Indian government's decision, not the Fund's — directly contradicting any reading in which the IMF pushed him out for criticising it; and no on-the-record government statement giving "misconduct" or any other formal reason has been found in accessible sources, nor has Subramanian himself been found on the record responding to either account (recorded as "No response recorded" per the contradiction rule).
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: An on-the-record statement from the Ministry of Finance, from the IMF beyond confirming who decided, or from Subramanian himself, giving a specific reason.

symmetryCheck: Applied to the Union-level control (UPA 2004-2014 vs NDA 2014-2026): the same World-Bank-sourced lens shows external debt growing under both dispensations without a partisan discontinuity that survives a base-rate check — nominal stock CAGR was higher in the UPA decade (approx 14.0%/yr, 2004-2014) than the NDA decade (approx 4.6%/yr, 2014-2024), which a naive reading could spin as "NDA more prudent," but the innocent reading (claim debt:c026) is that compounding off a roughly 3.7x-larger 2014 base mechanically produces a lower percentage growth rate even under identical policy, and the 2004-2014 window also contains the 2013 "taper tantrum" rupee shock, which moves a current-US$ figure independent of borrowing decisions. On the personnel side, RBI Governors and Finance Ministers were appointed by both UPA and NDA governments across this file's window without any observable pattern in the debt trajectory tracking the appointing party. This file could NOT run the two other mandatory controls (BJP-run vs opposition-run state borrowing; Chinese finance to private companies vs Japanese ODA to public projects) — both require data this file did not fetch and are left to the companion finance-fleet files, recorded as gaps above.
